tabs.title: Installations
tabs.story: Our journey starts in an empty folder. Before any 3D appears, we set up a tiny workshop: two files and one script tag that brings Babylon.js in from a CDN.

more.p: The CDN link above always serves the latest release. Search the docs for how to load a specific version, so a future update can’t change how your site behaves.

sections.p: Don’t want to set anything up? The Babylon.js Playground runs and shares snippets right in the browser. For a real project, follow the steps below.
Make a folder with two files: `index.html` for the page and `main.js` for your code. No installs and no build tools.
sections.code:
mkdir my-babylon-app
cd my-babylon-app
touch index.html main.js
sections.tip: You can also just create both files in your code editor.

sections.p: A CDN is a fast public server that hosts the library. One script tag downloads Babylon.js and creates a global object named `BABYLON`, so every class starts with `BABYLON.` and no `import` is needed.
sections.cap: Your page loads the CDN script, then your own script
sections.code:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang='en'>
<head>
  <meta charset='UTF-8'>
  <meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0'>
  <title>Babylon.js Tutorial</title>
</head>
<body>
  <script src='https://cdn.babylonjs.com/babylon.js'></script>
  <script src='main.js'></script>
</body>
</html>
sections.tip: Load Babylon.js first and your own script second. `main.js` needs `BABYLON` to exist already.

sections.p: Put this line in `main.js`, open `index.html` in your browser and look at the console.
sections.code: console.log(BABYLON.Engine.Version); // prints the Babylon.js version

sections.p: Opening the file directly works for now. Later, loading images, fonts, models and sounds needs a local server, because browsers block those requests on `file://` pages. Any one of these is enough; then open `http://localhost:8000`.
sections.code:
# Python
python3 -m http.server 8000

# or Node
npx serve .

# or use the Live Server extension in VS Code
sections.tip: Live Server also reloads the page every time you save.

tabs.title: The 4 Horsemen
tabs.story: Every Babylon.js app, however big, rides on the same four things. We meet them one by one and end with a working first scene.

more.p: Call `engine.getFps()` to see how many frames per second your scene really draws. We show it on screen in the GUI tab.

sections.p: The `<canvas>` is the space on your page. The Engine is the brain that turns your logic into 3D graphics. The Scene is the 3D space. The Camera shows one area of that space.
sections.cap: The four building blocks of every app

sections.p: Place it before the script tags.
sections.code:
<body>
  <canvas id='renderCanvas'></canvas>
  <script src='https://cdn.babylonjs.com/babylon.js'></script>
  <script src='main.js'></script>
</body>

sections.p: In `main.js`, grab the canvas and give it to the engine so it knows where to draw. There is no `import`: the CDN script already made `BABYLON` available.
sections.code:
const canvas = document.getElementById('renderCanvas');
const engine = new BABYLON.Engine(canvas);

sections.p: Put all your app logic in a `createScene` function that returns a scene. Calling `render()` draws one frame.
Animation, in a video or a game, is a sequence of pictures called frames. One `render()` call gives a still image. A render loop calls it many times per second, as fast as the device allows.
sections.cap: Many frames per second make motion
sections.tip: Congratulations: your first app is running! The console warns that the camera is missing, so we fix that next.

sections.p: Babylon.js can make a default camera and light for you. We study real cameras later. Add this inside `createScene()`.
sections.code: scene.createDefaultCameraOrLight(true, false, true);

sections.p: A little CSS in the `<head>` makes the canvas fill the page.
Resize the window and a cube would stretch. Tell the engine each time the window changes size.
Make `main.js` look like this. Every later tab adds code where it says `the fun stuff`.

tabs.title: MeshBuilder
tabs.story: The stage is ready but empty. MeshBuilder is the workshop that fills it. Every call has the same shape: a name, an options object and the scene.

more.p: Merging is great for things that never move. For many identical, movable copies (trees, bullets), search the docs for `createInstance`: copies share one geometry and are very cheap.

sections.p: Any object in a scene is a mesh: a simple box, a torus knot, or a complex model from Blender. `MeshBuilder` is a helper class that builds common ones in one line. We build five; explore the others as homework.
sections.cap: Three of the shapes we build

sections.p: The name helps you find the mesh later (we use it for picking). Raise `segments` for a smoother ball, and use `diameterY` to stretch one axis.
sections.cap: More segments means more triangles and more detail

sections.p: Use `size` for a cube, or `width`, `height` and `depth` one by one. `faceColors` paints each face. A Color4 has red, green, blue and opacity; Color3 skips opacity.
sections.tip: The scene argument is optional when your app has only one scene.

sections.p: A flat rectangle with a width and height. `subdivisions` cuts it into a grid, like a sphere’s segments. You can’t see the grid until you switch on wireframe. Use `subdivisionsX` and `subdivisionsY` for different counts.
sections.cap: Subdivisions matter when you move vertices to shape terrain

sections.p: A height map is a grayscale image: the whiter a pixel, the higher the point; the blacker, the lower. Put the image in `images/` and pass its path.
sections.cap: Brightness in the image turns into height
sections.tip: Default subdivisions is 1, so raise it to see detail, but more subdivisions cost more performance. `minHeight` and `maxHeight` set the altitude range.

sections.p: 3D text needs a font in JSON format (convert a `.ttf` with a tool like Facetype.js and put it in a `fonts` folder) plus the `earcut` library, which cuts letter shapes into triangles. Add its CDN script to `index.html`, before `main.js`.
sections.code:
<script src='https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/earcut/2.2.4/earcut.min.js'></script>
<script src='https://cdn.babylonjs.com/babylon.js'></script>
<script src='main.js'></script>

sections.p: Loading the font is asynchronous, so `createScene` becomes `async` and the render loop starts once the scene is ready. The arguments are: name, text, font data, options and scene. Babylon.js finds the global `earcut` by itself.
sections.tip: Use your own converted font file name instead of `GreatVibes.json`.

sections.p: `diameterTop` and `diameterBottom` set the two ends. Set `diameterTop` to 0 and the cylinder becomes a cone. `tessellation` is the number of sides.
sections.cap: Cylinder, torus and plane

sections.p: A torus is a donut: `diameter` is the whole ring and `thickness` is the tube. A torus knot is a twisted donut; `p` and `q` change how it twists.
A plane is a flat sheet, handy for signs and mirrors. It is only visible from the front unless you ask for both sides. A disc is a flat circle.
A pill shape, often used as a simple character body. `height` is the total height and `radius` is how round the ends are.

Every mesh costs the graphics card one ‘draw call’, so hundreds of separate meshes can slow your app. `MergeMeshes` glues many meshes into one new mesh, which is much cheaper to draw. The originals are removed.
sections.cap: Fewer meshes means fewer draw calls
sections.tip: Parts of a merged mesh can’t move on their own, and they share one material (see the next step).

sections.p: Pass more arguments to control the merge. Each one is explained below.
sections.code: const merged = BABYLON.Mesh.MergeMeshes([a, b, c], true, true, undefined, false, true);
list: `true`: remove the original meshes.
`true`: allow very large meshes (32-bit indices).
`undefined`: make a normal Mesh.
`false`: don’t split into sub-meshes.
`true`: keep each mesh’s own material.

tabs.title: Cameras
tabs.story: Shapes are on stage, so we choose how the audience looks. We meet one camera at a time: first how to create it, then its properties one by one.

more.p: Cameras read the keyboard, mouse and touch through ‘inputs’. Search the docs for camera inputs to learn how to change keys, add a gamepad, or remove an input.

sections.p: Every camera needs a name, a position (or angles) and the scene. Call `attachControl()` so it reacts to mouse, keys and touch. Only one camera is active at a time.
A first-person camera: the mouse sets the direction and the arrow keys move. Remove the default camera and add a default light first.
sections.cap: Walk around, or orbit a target

sections.p: One property per line:
sections.code:
camera.speed = 0.3;               // how fast it moves
camera.angularSensibility = 4000; // mouse look: higher = slower turning
camera.inertia = 0.9;             // 0 stops at once, 0.9 glides
camera.fov = 0.8;                 // field of view in radians (zoom)
camera.minZ = 0.1;                // nearest thing it can see
camera.maxZ = 100;                // farthest thing it can see
camera.keysUp = [87];             // W moves forward
camera.keysDown = [83];           // S moves back
camera.keysLeft = [65];           // A moves left
camera.keysRight = [68];          // D moves right

sections.h: Universal Camera: walk on the ground
sections.p: Collisions stop the camera from walking through meshes, and gravity makes it fall onto the floor.
It orbits a target. The arguments are: name, alpha (left-right angle), beta (up-down angle), radius (distance), target and scene.
One property per line:
sections.code:
camera.alpha = Math.PI / 2;        // turn left or right around the target
camera.beta = Math.PI / 3;         // 0 = from above, PI/2 = from the side
camera.radius = 10;                // distance from the target
camera.target = BABYLON.Vector3.Zero(); // the point it orbits
camera.wheelPrecision = 50;        // mouse wheel zoom: higher = slower
camera.panningSensibility = 1000;  // right-drag pan: higher = slower, 0 = off
camera.lowerRadiusLimit = 4;       // closest zoom
camera.upperRadiusLimit = 20;      // farthest zoom
camera.lowerBetaLimit = 0.1;       // can’t look straight down
camera.upperBetaLimit = Math.PI / 2; // can’t go below the ground
camera.useAutoRotationBehavior = true; // slow automatic spin

sections.p: It chases a mesh from behind, like in a driving or third-person game. Give it a start position, then lock it onto a target.
sections.cap: The camera keeps a distance and height from its target

sections.p: One property per line:
sections.code:
camera.lockedTarget = box;        // the mesh to follow
camera.radius = 10;               // distance from the target
camera.heightOffset = 4;          // how high above the target
camera.rotationOffset = 180;      // angle around the target in degrees (180 = behind)
camera.cameraAcceleration = 0.05; // how quickly it catches up (small = smooth)
camera.maxCameraSpeed = 10;       // speed limit while catching up

sections.p: Moves like an aircraft: it can fly in any direction and lean into turns.
One property per line:
sections.code:
camera.speed = 0.5;                    // flying speed
camera.rollCorrect = 10;               // how fast it levels the horizon again
camera.bankedTurn = true;              // lean into turns
camera.bankedTurnLimit = Math.PI / 2;  // maximum lean angle
camera.bankedTurnMultiplier = 1;       // how strongly it leans

sections.p: A normal camera shows perspective: far things look small. An orthographic camera shows everything at true size, like a map or a 2D game.
Detach the old camera, set the new one as active, attach it.

tabs.title: Materials
tabs.story: Our shapes are bare. A mesh is made of points and lines that give it shape, plus a material that covers them. Colors and textures live in the material.

more.p: `StandardMaterial` is simple. `PBRMaterial` uses metallic and roughness values to look like real metal, plastic or wood. Search the docs for PBR.

sections.p: Create a `StandardMaterial` and assign it. Nothing changes yet, but now we can restyle the sphere.
sections.cap: Shape + material = what you see

sections.p: `diffuseColor` is the main color. `specularColor` colors the highlight spot made by a light. Both depend on a light; with no light you get a dark object.
sections.code:
sphereMaterial.diffuseColor = new BABYLON.Color3(0.9, 0.2, 0.4);
sphereMaterial.specularColor = new BABYLON.Color3(0, 1, 0);

sections.p: `ambientColor` only works if the scene’s `ambientColor` has non-zero values in the same channels. `emissiveColor` colors the mesh even without light. `alpha` sets opacity. `wireframe` shows the mesh’s skeleton.
Set `diffuseTexture` for a picture that needs light. Use `emissiveTexture` if the picture should show without any light.
sections.tip: Put your own image in `images/`, and use your file name.

sections.h: A different picture on each face
sections.p: Cut one long image into six blocks. Each block is a Vector4 holding its lower-left and upper-right corners. Add `wrap: true` or the pieces appear flipped.
sections.cap: faceUV maps image blocks to box faces

sections.p: `uOffset` and `vOffset` slide the texture sideways or up and down. `uScale` and `vScale` shrink it to fit the mesh, or repeat it when above 1.
sections.code:
const tex = groundMaterial.emissiveTexture;

tex.uOffset = 1.4;  // move left or right
tex.vOffset = 1.4;  // move up or down

tex.uScale = 3;     // repeat 3 times across
tex.vScale = 2;     // repeat 2 times along

tabs.title: Transformations and Gizmos
tabs.story: New meshes appear at (0, 0, 0). We learn the three dials (position, rotation, scaling) one by one, then use gizmos to turn them with the mouse.

more.p: `rotation` can get stuck in odd cases (‘gimbal lock’). Search the docs for `rotationQuaternion` to learn the more robust way to rotate meshes.

sections.p: Position is a Vector3: x goes right, y goes up, z goes into the screen. Change one axis, or set all three.
sections.code:
box.position.x = 1;
box.position = new BABYLON.Vector3(-0.5, 0.2, 0.1);
sections.cap: The three axes and the three dials

sections.p: Rotation is in radians: `Math.PI` is 180 degrees. x tilts forward, y turns left or right, z rolls sideways.
1 is the normal size. 2 is twice as big, 0.5 is half. A negative value flips the mesh.
A gizmo is a set of drag handles on a mesh. Position, rotation and scale each have their own. They are handy for debugging and finding the right numbers.
They work the same way: create, then attach to a mesh.
sections.tip: Try one gizmo at a time to keep the scene readable.

sections.p: A `UtilityLayerRenderer` is a second, hidden scene drawn on top of your real scene. Gizmos live there, so they are never hidden behind meshes and don’t clutter your scene.
sections.cap: Gizmos are drawn in a separate layer on top
list: Always visible: meshes can’t cover the handles.
Separate: gizmos don’t appear in your scene’s mesh list.
Own lighting: your lights and shadows don’t affect them.
Cleanup: call `dispose()` when you no longer need it.

tabs.title: Animation
tabs.story: Back to the render loop. Animation is changing a number a little every frame. We go step by step, from the easiest method to the most flexible, then look at what can be animated.

more.p: An `AnimationGroup` bundles several animations (even on different meshes) so you can play, pause or stop them together. Model files use them too.

sections.p: An animation changes one property over time. Before writing code, answer four questions:
sections.cap: Keyframes are the dots; Babylon.js fills in between
list: What changes? A property such as `rotation.y` or `position`.
From which value to which value?
How fast? That’s frames per second (fps).
How long? Total frames ÷ fps = seconds (120 frames at 30 fps = 4 seconds).

sections.h: Method 1, step 1: change a number every frame
sections.p: The easiest way. `registerBeforeRender` runs your function before every frame, so a small change each time looks like movement.

sections.h: Method 1, step 2: same speed on every device
sections.p: Fast screens draw more frames, so the box would spin faster. Multiply by the time between frames to fix that.
One call does everything. The arguments, in order:
list: name: any label you like.
target: the mesh (or material) to animate.
property: the path, such as `'position.x'` or `'scaling'`.
fps, total frames, from, to.
Optional: loop mode, then an easing function.

sections.p: The full control version. First describe what is animated: a name, the property, the fps, the data type and the loop mode.
A keyframe is a frame number plus the value at that frame. Babylon.js fills in every frame between them. Want it slower? Use a bigger frame number.
Give the animation to the mesh, then begin it.
list: box: what to animate.
0, 60: first and last frame to play.
true: loop it.

sections.h: Types of animation: what can change
sections.p: The animated value can be a number, a vector or a color. With one-line animations, just pass different from and to values.
The loop mode decides what happens when the animation reaches its end.
Without easing, motion is steady. Easing makes it start slowly, end softly, bounce or snap.
list: `SineEase`, `QuadraticEase`, `CircleEase`: gentle starts and stops.
`BounceEase`: bounces at the end.
`ElasticEase`: springs like rubber.
`BackEase`: pulls back before moving.

sections.p: `beginAnimation` returns an object you can use to pause, restart, stop or speed it up.

tabs.title: Lights
tabs.story: A scene without light is a dark room. Good lighting changes everything, and Babylon.js offers four types. For these experiments, use a clean scene with an ArcRotateCamera and a ground, and no default light.

more.p: A light can be told to light only some meshes. Search the docs for `includedOnlyMeshes` and `excludedMeshes`.

sections.p: Point lights shine in every direction, spotlights in a cone, directional lights send parallel rays, and hemispheric lights give soft ambient light.
sections.cap: The four light types

sections.p: It shines in all directions, like a candle. It takes a name, a position and the scene. A `LightGizmo` shows where the light is.
A cone of light, like theatre lighting. Arguments: name, position, direction, cone angle, decay with distance, scene. `range` is the farthest it reaches.
Parallel rays from one direction, like the sun far away. It needs only a name, a direction and the scene.
Soft light from sky and ground. The direction points to the sky. `groundColor` lights the opposite side, `diffuse` is the main color and `specular` colors the highlights.

tabs.title: Shadow and Fog
tabs.story: Light needs shadows to feel real, and once both are in place, fog finishes the mood. First the shadow, step by step; then fog.

more.p: For big outdoor scenes one shadow map is too blurry. Search the docs for `CascadedShadowGenerator`, which uses several maps at different distances.

sections.p: In real life an object blocks light, and the surface behind it stays darker. In Babylon.js we recreate this with three actors. If one is missing, there is no shadow.
sections.cap: Light, caster, receiver: all three are needed
list: Light: the source of the shadow.
Caster: the mesh that blocks the light (the sphere).
Receiver: the mesh the shadow falls on (the ground).

sections.h: Step 1: pick a light that can cast shadows
sections.p: Directional, Spot and Point lights can cast shadows. A Hemispheric light can’t, because it has no single direction.
One generator per light. The first argument is the size of the shadow map: bigger is sharper but slower. The second is the light.
sections.code: const shadowGenerator = new BABYLON.ShadowGenerator(1024, light);

sections.h: Step 3: say who casts and who receives
sections.p: A mesh can be both.
sections.code:
shadowGenerator.addShadowCaster(sphere); // casts a shadow
ground.receiveShadows = true;            // shows shadows
sections.tip: Nothing appears? Check that the caster was added and `receiveShadows` is true on the receiver.

sections.p: Raw shadows look hard and blocky. Each line below improves them in a different way.
Check these common problems:
list: No shadow at all: is the light hemispheric, or is `receiveShadows` off?
Stripes on surfaces: increase `shadowGenerator.bias` a little, for example `0.0005`.
Blocky edges: use a bigger map size (2048) or add blur.
Shadow too dark or too light: change `setDarkness`.

sections.p: Fog fades meshes into a color the farther they are from the camera. It hides the far distance and adds atmosphere. There are four modes: none, linear, exp and exp2.
Fog grows steadily with distance. `fogStart` is where it begins and `fogEnd` is where objects vanish completely.
sections.cap: The farther away, the thicker the fog

sections.p: EXP and EXP2 thicken faster with distance (EXP2 faster still). They use a density instead of a start and end.
sections.code:
scene.fogMode = BABYLON.Scene.FOGMODE_EXP;   // or FOGMODE_EXP2
scene.fogDensity = 0.2;

sections.p: Match the fog to your background and distant objects melt away.
sections.code:
scene.fogColor = new BABYLON.Color3(0.3, 0.2, 0.6);
scene.clearColor = new BABYLON.Color4(0.3, 0.2, 0.6, 1); // same color

tabs.title: GUI
tabs.story: So far everything lives in 3D space. Games and apps also need flat 2D things on top: scores, buttons, sliders and labels. The Babylon.js GUI draws them over your scene.

more.p: The GUI above is flat and fixed to the screen. Search the docs for `GUI3DManager` to place buttons floating in 3D space, which is useful for VR.

sections.p: The GUI is a transparent 2D sheet laid over the canvas. You add controls to it: text, buttons, sliders, images and containers.
sections.cap: 2D controls on top of the 3D scene

sections.p: It is a separate CDN file. Add it after Babylon.js.
sections.code:
<script src='https://cdn.babylonjs.com/babylon.js'></script>
<script src='https://cdn.babylonjs.com/gui/babylon.gui.min.js'></script>
<script src='main.js'></script>

sections.p: Every control is added to this layer with `addControl`.
sections.code: const ui = BABYLON.GUI.AdvancedDynamicTexture.CreateFullscreenUI('UI');

sections.p: Name first, then the text. Controls sit in the center by default.
Use `onPointerUpObservable` to run code when it is clicked.
Sizes can be pixels (`'40px'`) or percentages of the screen (`'30%'`). Alignment sticks a control to a side, and `left` and `top` then push it away from that side.
A StackPanel places its children one under another (or in a row with `isVertical = false`).

sections.h: Step 7: arrange controls in a Grid
sections.p: Define columns and rows as fractions of the grid, then place each control by row and column.
They run a function whenever their value changes. Here they control a mesh.
`InputText` lets the visitor type. `Image` shows a picture from your `images` folder.
Change `text` inside the render loop to build a live score or an FPS counter.

sections.h: Step 11: stick a label to a mesh
sections.p: `linkWithMesh` makes a control follow a 3D mesh, perfect for name tags.

tabs.title: Picking Objects (Raycast)
tabs.story: Now we make the world interactive. When you click, Babylon.js shoots an invisible ray into the scene and tells you what it hit. We build this up one small step at a time.

more.p: Rays give you full control. For simple jobs like ‘do this when the mesh is clicked or hovered’, search the docs for `ActionManager`, which needs no picking code.

sections.p: A ray is an invisible line that starts at a point and goes in one direction, like a laser pointer. When you click, Babylon.js shoots a ray from the camera through the click position and reports the first mesh it touches. This is called picking.
sections.cap: A click becomes a ray that returns the mesh it hits

sections.p: A pointer event is a mouse click or a screen tap. First prove the click is detected.
`scene.pointerX` and `scene.pointerY` are the click position on the canvas. `scene.pick` shoots the ray from there and returns the result.
The result (a `PickingInfo`) tells you what happened. Always check `hit.hit` first.
list: `hit.hit`: true if the ray touched something.
`hit.pickedMesh`: the mesh that was touched.
`hit.pickedPoint`: the exact 3D point of the touch.
`hit.distance`: how far that point is from the camera.

sections.h: Step 4: react to the mesh you hit
sections.p: Compare the mesh name to decide what to do. This is why we name our meshes.
sections.tip: Without the `hit.hit` check, clicking empty space causes an error.

sections.h: Step 5: choose what can be picked
sections.p: Turn picking off for one mesh, or pass a function that decides for every mesh.

sections.h: Step 6: place an object where you click
sections.p: `pickedPoint` is a real 3D position, so you can put a new mesh exactly there.

sections.h: Step 7: react when the pointer moves
sections.p: `onPointerMove` works the same way. Here the cursor becomes a hand over any mesh.
You don’t need a click. Make a ray from any origin and direction, draw it with a helper, and pick with it. Useful to check what is below a character or in front of it.

tabs.title: Loading and Animating Models
tabs.story: Real projects rarely build everything from primitives. They load models made in Blender or downloaded from the web, often with animations. We start with the smallest possible import and add one idea at a time.

more.p: Large models download slowly. Search the docs for Draco compression, which shrinks `.glb` files a lot.

sections.p: `.glb` and `.gltf` files need the loaders script from the CDN, after Babylon.js and before `main.js`.
sections.code:
<script src='https://cdn.babylonjs.com/babylon.js'></script>
<script src='https://cdn.babylonjs.com/loaders/babylonjs.loaders.min.js'></script>
<script src='main.js'></script>
sections.cap: A model file goes through a loader into your scene

sections.p: Create a `models` folder next to `index.html` and put your `.glb` file in it. A `.glb` packs the model, textures and animations into one file, so it is the easiest format. Run a local server (see Installations).
`ImportMeshAsync` loads a model without freezing the page. It needs the folder, the file name and the scene. The empty string means ‘load every mesh in the file’.
sections.code: BABYLON.SceneLoader.ImportMeshAsync('', 'models/', 'Fox.glb', scene);
sections.tip: Nothing visible? Check the console for 404 errors, then try the next steps: the model may be too big or too small.

sections.h: Step 2: run code when it has loaded
sections.p: It returns a promise, so use `.then`. The result holds everything that was loaded.
`result.meshes[0]` is the root of the model, so changing it changes the whole model.
`result.animationGroups` holds the animations stored in the file. The first one usually starts playing by itself.

sections.h: Step 5: play the one you want
sections.p: Stop the default animation, find another by name, and play it. `true` means loop.
sections.tip: ‘Walk’ is a name from the fox model. Use the names printed in step 4.

sections.p: Replace the empty string with a list of mesh names from the file.
sections.code: BABYLON.SceneLoader.ImportMeshAsync(['Cube'], 'models/', 'Scene.glb', scene);

sections.p: An optional fifth argument is called while the file downloads.

sections.h: Older style: ImportMesh with a callback
sections.p: `ImportMesh` does the same job but gives you a callback instead of a promise.

tabs.title: Sound
tabs.story: A world feels empty without a soundtrack. Adding ambient music takes a single object.

more.p: Search the docs for `spatialSound` and `attachToMesh` to make a sound get louder as the camera comes closer to a mesh.

sections.p: Put your audio file in `audio/`. A `Sound` takes a name, the file path, the scene, a callback for when loading ends, and an options object.
sections.cap: Load a file, then loop it in the background
sections.tip: Browsers often block sound until the visitor interacts with the page.

sections.p: Skip `autoplay` and start or stop the sound from your own code, for example on a click.
The Sound class is simple and covers most needs.
list: Easy: one object with `autoplay`, `loop` and `volume` options.
Works with common formats like mp3, ogg and wav.
3D sound: with `spatialSound: true` a sound can come from a position in the scene.
Full control from code: play, pause, stop and change volume at any time.

sections.p: Know these before you plan your audio.
list: Browsers block sound until the visitor clicks or taps the page, so autoplay may stay silent at first.
Format support differs between browsers, so mp3 is the safest choice.
Big audio files load slowly and use memory.
Many sounds at once can hurt performance, especially on phones.
There is no built-in audio editing or advanced mixing.
Files should come from your own site, or a server that allows cross-origin loading.

tabs.title: Physics (Cannon.js)
tabs.story: So far objects only move when we tell them to. Physics lets the world take care of itself: things fall, bounce, push and topple. We use Cannon.js, a physics library that Babylon.js can plug in.

more.p: Newer Babylon.js versions use Havok, a faster physics engine with a newer API. Search the docs for ‘Babylon.js Havok physics’ when you outgrow Cannon.js.

sections.p: A physics engine calculates gravity, collisions and bounces for you. You describe each object (how heavy, how bouncy), and the engine moves it every frame.
sections.cap: Gravity pulls the ball down and restitution makes it bounce

sections.p: Add Cannon.js from a CDN before your own script.
sections.code:
<script src='https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/cannon.js/0.6.2/cannon.min.js'></script>
<script src='https://cdn.babylonjs.com/babylon.js'></script>
<script src='main.js'></script>
sections.tip: Cannon uses Babylon.js’s older physics system. If a very new Babylon.js version no longer includes it, load an older Babylon.js version from the CDN, or use Havok (see Read more).

sections.p: Give the scene a gravity vector and tell it to use Cannon. Earth’s gravity pulls down at about 9.81.

sections.h: Step 3: a floor that does not move
sections.p: A physics ‘impostor’ is the invisible shape the engine uses for a mesh. Mass 0 means the object never moves, perfect for a floor.
Give the sphere a mass above 0 and it falls on its own. Start it above the floor.
These three numbers change how an object behaves:
list: `mass`: how heavy. 0 means fixed in place.
`restitution`: bounciness. 0 = no bounce, 1 = bounces back to the same height.
`friction`: grip when sliding. 0 = ice, 1 = rubber.

sections.p: Pick the simplest shape that fits the mesh. Simple shapes are fast.
list: `BoxImpostor`: boxes, floors, walls.
`SphereImpostor`: balls.
`CylinderImpostor`: pillars, bowling pins.
`PlaneImpostor`: an endless flat floor.
`MeshImpostor`: the exact mesh shape. Accurate but slow, and only for fixed objects.

sections.p: Give the ball a sudden push (impulse), or set its speed directly.
Run code when one impostor hits another.

sections.h: Recipe: a tower to knock down
sections.p: Create boxes in a loop, give each a physics impostor, then hit the tower with the ball.

tabs.title: Particle Systems
tabs.story: Fire, smoke, sparks and magic are not solid meshes. They are thousands of tiny pictures that are born, move and fade. A particle system makes them. We build one, then learn each control.

more.p: A normal system runs on the CPU. For hundreds of thousands of particles, search the docs for `GPUParticleSystem`, which runs on the graphics card.

sections.p: A particle system is a machine that keeps creating tiny pictures (particles). Each one is born at an emitter, moves, ages and dies. You control where, how many, how long, how fast and what color.
sections.cap: Born, move, fade out

sections.p: Three things are needed: a texture (the picture of one particle), an emitter (where they are born) and `start()`.
sections.tip: 2000 is the most particles alive at once. Everything else has a default, so we tune it step by step.

sections.p: The emitter can be a point or a mesh (the particles then follow the mesh). An emit box spreads births over an area.
sections.code:
particles.emitter = box; // follows the mesh

particles.minEmitBox = new BABYLON.Vector3(-0.5, 0, -0.5); // one corner
particles.maxEmitBox = new BABYLON.Vector3(0.5, 0, 0.5);   // opposite corner

sections.p: Each particle gets a random color between `color1` and `color2`, fades to `colorDead`, and has a random size.
sections.code:
particles.color1 = new BABYLON.Color4(1, 0.6, 0.1, 1);  // start color A
particles.color2 = new BABYLON.Color4(1, 0.2, 0, 1);    // start color B
particles.colorDead = new BABYLON.Color4(0, 0, 0, 0);   // end color (invisible)
particles.minSize = 0.1;                                // smallest particle
particles.maxSize = 0.4;                                // biggest particle
particles.blendMode = BABYLON.ParticleSystem.BLENDMODE_ONEONE; // glowing blend

sections.h: Step 4: how many and how long
sections.p: Particles alive at once are about `emitRate × lifetime`. Keep that below the maximum you set.
sections.code:
particles.emitRate = 300;       // new particles per second
particles.minLifeTime = 0.5;    // shortest life in seconds
particles.maxLifeTime = 1.5;    // longest life in seconds

sections.p: Directions are two corners; each particle picks a random direction between them. Power is the start speed, and gravity pulls them over time.

sections.h: Step 6: start, stop and clean up
sections.p: You decide when the system runs.
Instead of a stream, release a fixed number of particles at once.
sections.code:
particles.manualEmitCount = 100; // release 100 at once
particles.start();

sections.p: Combine the steps: upward directions, warm colors, a glowing blend and many short-lived particles.
Combine particles with picking: move the emitter to the clicked point, then burst.

tabs.title: Tools
tabs.story: One thing that sets Babylon.js apart is its tool set. These tools make debugging easier and let you share work with the community.

more.p: Building a GUI by hand takes many lines. Search for the Babylon.js GUI Editor to design screens visually and export them.

sections.p: The Playground (used all through the original tutorial) writes and shares snippets online. The Inspector, Sandbox and Node Material Editor cover debugging, previewing and shaders.
sections.cap: Debug, preview, and build shaders without code

sections.p: A visual panel to explore and edit your scene live: objects, textures, materials and animations. You can take screenshots, record video, and export the scene as `.babylon` or `.gltf`.
Drop a model into the Sandbox to preview and inspect it before you use it in a project.
Build shaders by connecting nodes, with no code at all. Shaders are an advanced topic for another day.
sections.tip: A shader is a small program that tells the graphics card how to color each pixel.

tabs.title: Final Thoughts
tabs.story: We started in an empty folder and now have shapes, cameras, materials, motion, lights, shadows, fog, GUI, clicks, models, sound, physics and particles. Here is where to keep learning.

more.p: Babylon.js can run in virtual and augmented reality. Search the docs for `WebXR` to see how little code a VR scene needs.

sections.p: This is only the surface of Babylon.js, so keep experimenting. Build the exercises in the next tab, then try your own ideas.
Bookmark these.

links.d: write, run and share code in the browser.
ask questions; the community and the core team are friendly.
drop a model to preview it.

tabs.title: Exercises
tabs.story: Reading is not enough: build things. Each exercise says what to make, lists the requirements to tick off, and points to the tab to reread. Do them in order, or jump to your weak area.

sections.p: Create a fresh project and prove that Babylon.js is loaded.
sections.tip: Hint (Installations): `BABYLON.Engine.Version` and `document.getElementById('version').textContent`.
list: A folder with `index.html` and `main.js`.
Load Babylon.js from the CDN before `main.js`.
Show the version in the console AND inside a `<div id='version'>` on the page.
Open it through a local server.

sections.h: Exercise 2: An empty scene that behaves
sections.p: Make the starter template yours.
sections.tip: Hint (The 4 Horsemen): Reread the full-screen CSS and `engine.resize()`.
list: The canvas fills the whole window.
Dark blue background using `scene.clearColor`.
Default camera and light, with one sphere in the middle.
Resizing the window must not stretch the sphere.

sections.p: Use at least four shape types.
sections.tip: Hint (MeshBuilder): A cone is `CreateCylinder` with `diameterTop: 0`; use `DOUBLESIDE` for planes.
list: Box walls, a cone roof, a plane door and a ground.
Give every mesh a name.
Every part must touch the ground or the wall, with no gaps.
Make the door visible from both sides.

sections.p: Build one lamp and repeat it cheaply.
sections.tip: Hint (MeshBuilder): `BABYLON.Mesh.MergeMeshes` and `mesh.clone()`.
list: A lamp is a thin cylinder (pole) plus a sphere (bulb), merged into one mesh.
Clone it 5 times, 2 units apart.
Merge all 6 lamps into one mesh.
Print `scene.meshes.length` before and after merging.

sections.p: Switch between camera types with the keyboard.
sections.tip: Hint (Cameras): `window.addEventListener('keydown', ...)` and `scene.activeCamera`.
list: Scene with a ground and a moving box.
Keys 1 to 4 select Universal, Arc Rotate, Follow and Fly cameras.
Detach the old camera and attach the new one.
Log the active camera name on each switch.

sections.p: Make a dice and a textured floor.
sections.tip: Hint (Materials): `faceColors`, `diffuseTexture`, `uScale`.
list: A box with a different color on each face, or `faceUV` with one image.
A ground with a repeating texture (`uScale` and `vScale` of 4).
A sphere that glows with `emissiveColor`.
One mesh with `alpha` of 0.5.

sections.p: Show how parenting works.
sections.tip: Hint (Transformations): `mesh.parent`, `rotation.y` in `registerBeforeRender`, `PositionGizmo`.
list: A sun in the center, a planet and a moon.
The planet is a child of the sun, the moon a child of the planet.
Each body spins at its own speed.
Attach a position gizmo to the sun and drag it: everything must follow.

sections.p: Use three animation methods in one scene.
sections.tip: Hint (Animation): Keep the object returned by `beginAnimation` so you can call `pause()` and `restart()`.
list: The box moves up and down with YOYO loop mode and a `BounceEase`.
Its color animates from red to blue.
It spins continuously with `registerBeforeRender`.
The P key pauses and resumes the position animation.

sections.p: Switch the whole mood with one key.
sections.tip: Hint (Lights): `light.intensity`, `scene.clearColor`, `light.setEnabled()`.
list: A hemispheric light for the sky and a directional light for the sun.
Pressing N lowers both intensities and makes the background dark.
A point light (a lamp) that only turns on at night.
Press N again to go back to day.

sections.p: Place many trees with shadows and fog.
sections.tip: Hint (Shadow and Fog): `Math.random()`, `addShadowCaster`, `FOGMODE_EXP`.
list: 20 trees (a cylinder trunk plus a sphere top) at random positions in a loop.
One directional light with a shadow generator and soft edges.
Every tree casts a shadow and the ground receives it.
Exponential fog whose color matches the background.

sections.p: Build a small panel that controls a box.
sections.tip: Hint (GUI): `AdvancedDynamicTexture`, `onPointerUpObservable`, `linkWithMesh`.
list: A text block showing `Score: 0` and a +1 button that raises the score.
A slider that rotates the box.
A checkbox that shows or hides the box.
A label that follows the box.

sections.p: Make the scene react to the pointer.
sections.tip: Hint (Picking (Raycast)): `scene.pick`, `hit.pickedPoint`, `canvas.style.cursor`.
list: Five boxes in a row. Clicking one gives it a random color.
The cursor becomes a hand only when over a box.
Clicking the ground drops a small sphere exactly at that point.
Use `isPickable` so spheres you dropped can’t be picked again.

sections.p: Load a `.glb` and control its animations.
sections.tip: Hint (Loading Models): Loop over `result.animationGroups` and create a button for each.
list: Import the model with `ImportMeshAsync` and scale it to fit.
Log the animation names.
Create one GUI button per animation; clicking plays that animation.
Show the loading percentage in the console.

sections.p: Control music from the screen.
sections.tip: Hint (Sound): `autoplay: false` and the Limitations section.
list: Play, Pause and Stop buttons made with the GUI.
A slider that changes the volume (`setVolume`).
The music must not start until the first click.
Write one sentence in a comment explaining why.

sections.p: Spawn balls with physics.
sections.tip: Hint (Physics): `registerOnPhysicsCollide` and GUI text.
list: A static ground.
Each click spawns a ball above the clicked point.
Give each ball a different `restitution`.
Count the collisions with the ground and show the number on the screen.

sections.p: Knock down pins.
sections.tip: Hint (Physics): `CylinderImpostor`, `applyImpulse`, check `pin.position.y`.
list: Ten cylinder pins in a triangle.
A ball that rolls when you press Space (apply an impulse).
Pins must fall and push each other.
Show how many pins are lying down afterwards.

sections.p: Make a burst appear where you click.
sections.tip: Hint (Particles): `manualEmitCount`, `targetStopDuration`, `disposeOnStop`.
list: Click a point to release 100 particles there.
Each burst uses a random color.
Gravity pulls the sparks down.
The system removes itself after 2 seconds.

sections.p: Combine fire, light and a ground.
sections.tip: Hint (Particles and Lights): `Math.random()` in `registerBeforeRender`, `scene.debugLayer.show()`.
list: A fire particle system on a few log boxes.
A point light at the fire that flickers (random intensity every frame).
Fog and a dark sky.
Open the Inspector and tweak the light intensity live.

sections.p: Let a visitor inspect a product.
sections.tip: Hint (Cameras, Materials and GUI): `useAutoRotationBehavior`, `diffuseColor`, `setPosition`.
list: An Arc Rotate camera with zoom and angle limits.
It rotates by itself until the visitor drags it.
Three color buttons that change the model’s material.
A Reset button that moves the camera back.

sections.p: Finish with a small game that uses many tabs.
sections.tip: Hint (Everything): `intersectsMesh` to detect touching, plus everything above.
list: A ball moves with the W, A, S, D keys (physics or direct movement).
A Follow camera chases the ball.
Ten spinning coins (tori) are placed at random.
Touching a coin removes it, plays a sound and bursts particles.
A GUI score counts the coins, and a message appears when all are collected.
